metadata.document: SUBMISSION ON THE RESOURCE MANAGEMENT (ENABLING HOUSING SUPPLY AND OTHER MATTERS) AMENDMENT BILL

cleaned_body_text: This is a submission on the Resource Management (Enabling Housing Supply and Other Matters) Amendment Bill (the Bill). The Bill seeks to amend the Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA) to rapidly accelerate the supply of developable residential land where demand for housing is high. The Environmental Defence Society Incorporated (EDS) is a not-for-profit, non-government national environmental organisation. It was established in 1971 with the objective of bringing together the disciplines of law, science, and planning in order to promote better environmental outcomes in resource management. EDS supports the policy intent of the Bill, which we see as the need to provide for density in existing urban areas. This should prevent urban sprawl, which is generally detrimental to environmental wellbeing and should be controlled. However, this support is qualified. At the highest level, we question the need for the Bill. We note that the National Policy Statement on Urban Development (NPSUD) is already driving an increase in development capacity. Rather than creating a parallel process, introducing blanket permitted activity standards, and creating additional complexity, a more appropriate approach would be to speed up the implementation of the existing NPSUD. However, if the Bill proceeds, it should focus on its core legitimate concern: to overcome objections to greater density and provide more development capacity for housing. This should not be conflated with the removal of design controls or a weakening of environmental safeguards. Poor urban design can lead to cities that are both less liveable and detrimental to the environment. Good urban design solutions become even more important with increased density. More specifically, EDS is concerned that the application of blanket permitted activity standards to provide for dense development does not encourage the many synergies that can and should be achieved by creating well-designed urban density. More design considerations should be included in the Bill's concept of qualifying matters which justify more stringent controls. The relationship between the Bill and other nationally important environmental instruments, such as the New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement and bespoke legislation for the Waitākere Ranges and the Hauraki Gulf, should be clarified. The legal test when determining whether default medium density residential standards should apply should be anchored in recognizing and providing for matters in section 6 of the RMA and giving effect to national policy statements. Careful consideration and clarification is required to determine what areas are deemed to be residential for the purpose of the Bill. It is also important that a clear distinction continue to be drawn between district and regional controls. In conclusion, EDS does not see the justification for such a far-reaching Bill and considers changes would be better contained in national direction rather than primary legislation. However, in the event the Bill proceeds, we have highlighted key changes regarding environmental safeguards and good urban design considerations.
